name: healing stones

attributes.attribute: boulders and pebbles with holes honored as healing objects in Celtic lands
patients passed through them to cure ailments from infancy, rheumatism, and measles
linked to Megalithic monuments and possibly pre-Celtic times
holed Irish stones valued across England and Scotland as especially effective healers
cured ailments when walked round three times deosil on Orkney

sources: Bord, Janet, and Colin Bord. The Secret Country: An interpretation of the folklore of ancient sites in the British Isles. New York: Walker and Co., 1976.
Grinsell, Leslie V. Folklore of Prehistoric Sites in Britain. London: David & Charles, 1976.
Meaden, George Terrence. The Goddess of the Stones: The Language of the Megaliths. London: Souvenir Press, 1991, 186.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Healing stones are Celtic ritual objects. Boulders and pebbles with holes were honored in many Celtic lands. The tradition is often tied to the monuments of the Megalithic civilization and may go back to pre-Celtic times. In Brittany people passed newborns through the hole in the stone at Fouvent-le-Haut. This protected them from the ailments of infancy and from the spells of evil witches. At Amance people threw money through a holed stone as a substitute for the child. In Cornwall the round rock at Men-an-Tol near Madron cured rheumatism. The patient crawled naked through the stone, or others pushed him through, while a spell was repeated a magical number of times, usually three or nine. In England the Long Stone of Gloucestershire cured children of measles, whooping cough, and other contagious disease. People who dropped through the Tolmen in Dartmoor into the North Teign River below were cured of arthritis. In Ireland children with rickets were passed through the Cloch-a-Phoill in Co. Carlow. Another huge stone at a triple crossroads in Co. Sligo, called Clochbhreach or Clochlia, had a natural perforation for children with measles. The Irish valued holed stones through England and Scotland as strong healers. One Irish rock in Northumberland never touched English soil, to keep its power, and worked best in Irish hands. In Scotland stitch-stones eased skin and chronic complaints. The healed kept a stone until the next sufferer called for it. The Stones of Stenness on Orkney cured many ills when one walked around them three times deosil, in the direction of the sun.

okr.objective: Document the holed healing stones and the rituals performed at them.
key_results: Record the stone ritual sites from Brittany and Cornwall to Ireland and Scotland.
Describe the passing-through rite and the magical repetition of spells.
Note the regional stones and the walk-around cure at Orkney.
